spans.quote: Welcoming efforts in this context by multilateral arrangements which contribute to non-proliferation, Affirming that prevention of proliferation of nuclear, chemical and biological weapons should not hamper international cooperation in materials, equipment and technology for peaceful purposes while goals of peaceful utilization should not be used as a cover for proliferation, Gravely concerned by the threat of terrorism and the risk that non-State actors* such as those identified in the United Nations list established and maintained by the Committee established under Security Council resolution 1267 and those to whom resolution 1373 applies, may acquire, develop, traffic in or use nuclear, chemical and biological weapons and their means of delivery, Gravely concerned by the threat of illicit trafficking in nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons and their means of delivery, and related materials,* which adds a new dimension to the issue of proliferation of such weapons and also poses a threat to international peace and security, Recognizing the need to enhance coordination of efforts on national, subregional, regional and international levels in order to strengthen a global response to this serious challenge and threat to international security, Recognizing that most States have undertaken binding legal obligations under treaties to which they are parties, or have made other commitments aimed at preventing the proliferation of nuclear, chemical or biological weapons, and have taken effective measures to account for, secure and physically protect sensitive materials, such as those required by the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Materials and those recommended by the IAEA Code of Conduct on the Safety and Security of Radioactive Sources, Recognizing further the urgent need for all States to take additional effective measures to prevent the proliferation of nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery, Encouraging all Member States to implement fully the disarmament treaties and agreements to which they are party, Reaffirming the need to combat by all means, in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, threats to international peace and security caused by terrorist acts, Determined to facilitate henceforth an effective response to global threats in the area of ## Answer

The Security Council, acting under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, decided in resolution 1540 (2004) that all States must refrain from providing any form of support to non-State actors attempting to develop, acquire, manufacture, possess, transport, transfer or use nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery [1]. The Council also decided that all States must adopt and enforce laws prohibiting non-State actors from engaging in these activities, and must establish domestic controls to prevent proliferation of such weapons [2].

Yes, these decisions are binding on States. The resolution was adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, and the operative paragraphs use the verb "Decides," which creates binding obligations on all UN Member States under Article 25 of the Charter [1].

---

## Legal position

Resolution 1540 (2004) is a Chapter VII binding decision. The Council acted under its enforcement powers to address what it determined to be a threat to international peace and security: the proliferation of nuclear, chemical and biological weapons and their means of delivery, particularly to non-State actors [1].

The binding operative paragraphs impose three core obligations on all States [3]:

1. No support to non-State actors (paragraph 1): States must refrain from providing any form of support to non-State actors attempting to acquire or use weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery [4].

2. Prohibitory legislation (paragraph 2): States must adopt and enforce laws prohibiting non-State actors from manufacturing, acquiring, possessing, developing, transporting, transferring or using nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery, particularly for terrorist purposes [5].

3. Domestic controls (paragraph 3): States must establish effective measures to account for, secure, and control related materials, including physical protection measures, border controls, and national export and trans-shipment controls [6].

Paragraph 5 clarifies that none of these obligations shall be interpreted so as to conflict with or alter the rights and obligations of States Parties to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention [7].

## Analysis

The Council's binding decisions on non-State actors and weapons of mass destruction are found in the operative paragraphs of resolution 1540 (2004), adopted on 28 April 2004. The resolution opens with the formula "Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations," which signals the Council's intention to create binding obligations [1].

Paragraph 1 uses the verb "Decides" followed by "that all States shall refrain from providing any form of support to non-State actors" attempting to develop, acquire, manufacture, possess, transport, transfer or use nuclear, chemical or biological weapons and their means of delivery [4].

Paragraph 2 similarly "Decides also that all States, in accordance with their national procedures, shall adopt and enforce appropriate effective laws which prohibit any non-State actor" from engaging in the prohibited activities [5].

Paragraph 3 "Decides also that all States shall take and enforce effective measures to establish domestic controls" including accounting for and securing related materials, physical protection measures, border controls, and export and trans-shipment controls [6].

The binding character derives from Article 25 of the UN Charter, under which Member States agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the Security Council. When the Council acts under Chapter VII and uses the verb "decides," it exercises its binding law-making power [9].

Paragraph 5 provides a safeguard: "Decides that none of the obligations set forth in this resolution shall be interpreted so as to conflict with or alter the rights and obligations of State Parties to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention" [7].

I'll research the Permanent Court of International Justice's case law on whether restrictions on State independence can be presumed.

## Answer

No. Under the Permanent Court of International Justice's case law, restrictions on the independence of States cannot be presumed [1]. The Court held in *Lotus* that "restrictions upon the independence of States cannot therefore be presumed" [2]. This principle reflects the fundamental nature of international law as a legal order governing relations between sovereign, independent States [3].

## Legal position

 Restrictions on that independence must be affirmatively established, not presumed [2].

## Relevant authorities

1. **Lotus, Judgment, 7 September 1927, P.C.I.J., Series A, No. 10** — persuasive; status not verified. The Court's majority judgment establishes that restrictions on State independence cannot be presumed, and that international law leaves States "a wide measure of discretion" limited only by prohibitive rules, [4].

2. **Customs Regime, Advisory Opinion, 5 September 1931, P.C.I.J., Series A/B, No. 41** — not binding (advisory opinion); status not verified. The Court distinguished between restrictions a State agrees to and alienation of independence, noting that "restrictions on its liberty of action which a State may agree to do not affect its independence" [5].

3. Wimbledon, Judgment, 17 August 1923, P.C.I.J., Series A, No. 1 — persuasive; status not verified. The Court held that treaty obligations placing restrictions on sovereignty do not constitute abandonment of sovereignty, stating that "the right of entering into international engagements is an attribute of State sovereignty" [6].

## Analysis

 The Court reasoned that because international law governs relations between independent States and its rules "emanate from their own free will," any restriction on that independence must be clearly established rather than presumed [7]. The Court explicitly rejected the argument that States need affirmative authorization to act; instead, States are free to act unless international law contains a prohibitive rule [8].

This principle emerged from competing views on jurisdiction [9]. France argued that Turkey needed a permissive rule authorizing its exercise of jurisdiction [10]. Turkey contended that jurisdiction was permissible unless a prohibitive rule existed [11]. The Court adopted Turkey's approach, finding that international law "leaves them in this respect a wide measure of discretion which is only limited in certain cases by prohibitive rules" [12].

The *Customs Regime* opinion reinforces this approach by distinguishing between restrictions that affect independence and those that do not [13]. The Court noted that treaty-based restrictions on liberty of action do not compromise independence, provided the State retains its "organic powers" [14]. This acknowledges that States may voluntarily accept limitations through treaty obligations while preserving their underlying sovereignty [15].

*Wimbledon* applied similar reasoning in holding that treaty obligations restricting the exercise of sovereign rights (such as keeping the Kiel Canal open to vessels of all nations) do not constitute abandonment of sovereignty [16]. The Court recognized that the capacity to undertake such obligations is itself an attribute of sovereignty [17].

Together, these authorities establish that:
- Restrictions on State independence require positive proof through treaty or custom [2]
- The presumption favors State freedom of action [18]
- Voluntary restrictions accepted by States through treaty do not negate independence [13]

I'll search for the controlling authority on whether oral declarations by foreign ministers bind their States.

**Answer**

Yes. An oral declaration by a foreign minister is binding on his State when made in response to a request by the diplomatic representative of a foreign Power regarding a question falling within his province [1].

**Legal position**

The controlling authority is the Permanent Court of International Justice's judgment in the *Eastern Greenland* case [2]. The Court held that a foreign minister's oral statement, made on behalf of his government in response to a diplomatic request within his competence, binds his State [1]. The Court treated the "Ihlen declaration" — a verbal statement by the Norwegian Minister for Foreign Affairs — as an unconditional and definitive undertaking that Norway could not later disavow [3].

**Relevant authority**

| Authority | Citation | Binding label | Reason | Status |
|-----------|----------|---------------|--------|--------|
| *Eastern Greenland*, Judgment, 5 April 1933, P.C.I.J., Series A/B, No. 53 | Majority opinion | Persuasive | No binding precedent (PCIJ Statute Art. 59); a subsidiary means of determining the law (Art. 38(1)(d)), of high weight | Status not verified |

**Analysis**

The Court's reasoning rests on the foreign minister's institutional authority [4] [1]. When M. Ihlen, the Norwegian Minister for Foreign Affairs, stated on 22 July 1919 that "the Norwegian Government would not make any difficulty in the settlement of this question" regarding Danish sovereignty over Greenland, the Court held this statement binding on Norway, [5] [6].

The Court articulated the principle in these terms: "a reply of this nature given by the Minister for Foreign Affairs on behalf of his Government in response to a request by the diplomatic representative of a foreign Power, in regard to a question falling within his province, is binding upon the country to which the Minister belongs" [1].

Two conditions emerge from the Court's formulation:
1. The declaration must be made "on behalf of his Government" — that is, within the foreign minister's representative capacity; and [7]
2. The subject matter must be "a question falling within his province" — that is, within the foreign minister's competence [1].

The Court further concluded that the declaration was "unconditional and definitive" and could not be replaced by a later position subject to reservations [8].

spans.title: Security Council resolution 1593 (2005) [on referring the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court]
spans.quote: The Security Council, Taking note of the report of the International Commission of Inquiry on violations of international humanitarian law and human rights law in Darfur (S/2005/60), Recalling article 16 of the Rome Statute under which no investigation or prosecution may be commenced or proceeded with by the International Criminal Court for a period of 12 months after a Security Council request to that effect, Also recalling articles 75 and 79 of the Rome Statute and encouraging States to contribute to the ICC Trust Fund for Victims, Taking note of the existence of agreements referred to in Article 98-2 of the Rome Statute, Determining that the situation in Sudan continues to constitute a threat to international peace and security, Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, 1.

spans.title: S/RES/1970 (2011), 26 February 2011
spans.quote: The Security Council, Expressing grave concern at the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya and condemning the violence and use of force against civilians, Deploring the gross and systematic violation of human rights, including the repression of peaceful demonstrators, expressing deep concern at the deaths of civilians, and rejecting unequivocally the incitement to hostility and violence against the civilian population made from the highest level of the Libyan government, Welcoming the condemnation by the Arab League, the African Union, and the Secretary General of the Organization of the Islamic Conference of the serious violations of human rights and international humanitarian law that are being committed in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, Taking note of the letter to the President of the Security Council from the Permanent Representative of the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya dated 26 February 2011, Welcoming the Human Rights Council resolution A/HRC/RES/S-15/1 of 25 February 2011, including the decision to urgently dispatch an independent international commission of inquiry to investigate all alleged violations of international human rights law in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, to establish the facts and circumstances of such violations and of the crimes perpetrated, and where possible identify those responsible, Considering that the widespread and systematic attacks currently taking place in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya against the civilian population may amount to crimes against humanity, Expressing concern at the plight of refugees forced to flee the violence in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya, Expressing concern also at the reports of shortages of medical supplies to treat the wounded,

I'll search for Security Council resolutions referring situations to the ICC and examine their binding nature.

## Answer

Yes, the Security Council has referred situations to the International Criminal Court (ICC) [1] [2]. There have been two referrals, both adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter and both binding [1] [3].

### The two Security Council referrals

**1.

On 31 March 2005, the Security Council adopted resolution 1593 (2005), deciding "to refer the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court" [4]. The resolution was adopted acting under Chapter VII, making the referral decision binding on Member States under Article 25 of the UN Charter [1].

**2.

On 26 February 2011, the Security Council adopted resolution 1970 (2011), deciding "to refer the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya since 15 February 2011 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court" [5]. This resolution was also adopted under Chapter VII, making it binding.

### Were the referrals binding?

Yes, both referrals were binding. Each resolution used the operative verb "Decides" in the referral paragraph and was adopted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter [5]. Under Article 25 of the Charter, decisions of the Security Council are binding on all UN Member States.

The binding nature is confirmed by:

- S/RES/1593 (2005), para. 1: "Decides to refer the situation in Darfur since 1 July 2002 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court" — labelled as "binding" because it is a "Decision adopted acting under Chapter VII; binding on Member States (UN Charter Art. 25)" [6].

- S/RES/1970 (2011), para. 4: "Decides to refer the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya since 15 February 2011 to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court" — labelled as "binding" for the same reason [5].

Both resolutions also imposed binding cooperation obligations on the concerned states (Sudan and Libya respectively) and all UN Member States [7] [8].

### Legal position

 A referral to the ICC constitutes such a measure, and the binding nature of these decisions flows from the Council's Chapter VII powers combined with Article 25 of the Charter [9] [1].

### Relevant authorities

|-----------|-----------|---------------|--------|
| S/RES/1593 (2005) | 31 March 2005 | Binding (Chapter VII decision) | Status not verified | [10]
| S/RES/1970 (2011) | 26 February 2011 | Binding (Chapter VII decision) | Status not verified | [11]

### Research log

**Collections searched**: UN Security Council resolutions held in the firm's research collection.

**Queries used**:
- "Security Council referral situation to International Criminal Court" [12]
- "refers situation in Libya to International Criminal Court" [13]

As-of date: 2 October 2026.

**Sources needed but not in collection**: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (to confirm Article 13(b) text directly); ICC jurisprudence on the effect of Security Council referrals.

I'll check the current mandate status of the UN Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement (UNMHA) using the available Security Council resolutions.

## Answer

No. The UN Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement (UNMHA) is no longer mandated as of today, 2 October 2026.

The Security Council terminated UNMHA's mandate through a series of resolutions [1]:

1. S/RES/2786 (2025) extended the mandate until 28 January 2026 [2].

2. S/RES/2813 (2026) then provided a final two-month extension until 31 March 2026, explicitly stating this was for the purpose of conducting "the effective, efficient and safe drawdown of the Mission including ceasing of its operations" [3]. The resolution further decided that "as of 1 April 2026, UNMHA will commence a liquidation process" [4].

3. The search of Security Council resolutions from March 2026 to October 2026 found no further action on UNMHA.

Accordingly, UNMHA's mandate expired on 31 March 2026, and the mission entered liquidation on 1 April 2026 [5].
